# Using a histogram as the graphical method to describe the data
# Following the rule of thumb on how many classes a histogram should have (MS page 33)

# Get the number of classes
if (length(galaxy$VELOCITY) < 25) {
  nclass <- 6
} else if (length(galaxy$VELOCITY) >= 25 &
           length(galaxy$VELOCITY) <= 50) {
  nclass <- 8
} else{
  nclass <- 12
}

# Plot the histogram
hist_gal <- hist(
  galaxy$VELOCITY,
  nclass = nclass,
  main = "Histogram of Galaxy Velocities",
  xlab = "Velocity",
  ylab = "Frequency"
)

# Get numerical summary of histogram

2.

Yes, upon inspecting the histogram made in part a. there is evidence to support the double cluster theory. The histogram appears to be bi-modal, meaning it has two peaks each with its own center, which indicates two separate clusters within the same data set.

3.

In order to separate the two clusters I will subset the data using a value in the “valley” between the two peaks on the histogram. For this I’ll pick 21250 as the separation value because it is between the two break points where the “valley” occurs.

# Subset the data into the two groups
cluster_a <- galaxy[galaxy$VELOCITY < 21250, ]
cluster_b <- galaxy[galaxy$VELOCITY > 21250, ]

Cluster A

# Histogram, boxplot and numerical descriptive measures for Cluster A

# Get the number of classes like before
if (length(cluster_a$VELOCITY) < 25) {
  nclass_a <- 6
} else if (length(cluster_a$VELOCITY) >= 25 &
           length(cluster_a$VELOCITY) <= 50) {
  nclass_a <- 8
} else{
  nclass_a <- 12
}

# Plot the histogram

  cluster_a$VELOCITY,
  nclass = nclass_a,
  main = "Histogram of Galaxy Velocities - Cluster A",
  xlab = "Velocity",
  ylab = "Frequency"
)

Side-by-Side

# Put the histograms side-by-side
par(mfrow = c(1, 2)) # make 1x2 grid for plots

# Cluster A
hist_gal_a <- hist(
  cluster_a$VELOCITY,
  nclass = nclass_a,
  main = "Cluster A",
  xlab = "Velocity",
  ylab = "Frequency"
)

# Cluster B
hist_gal_b <- hist(
  cluster_b$VELOCITY,
  nclass = nclass_b,
  main = "Cluster B",
  xlab = "Velocity",
  ylab = "Frequency"
)

par(mfrow = c(1, 1)) # reset plot grid

# Do the same for the boxplots but as one plot

# Add cluster ID to each subset and then combine into one dataframe
cluster_a$ID <- rep("A1775A", length(cluster_a$VELOCITY))
cluster_b$ID <- rep("A1775B", length(cluster_b$VELOCITY))
comb_cluster_AB <- rbind(cluster_a, cluster_b)

# Boxplot of clusters
boxplot(
  comb_cluster_AB$VELOCITY ~ comb_cluster_AB$ID,
  range = 3,
  xlab = "Cluster",
  ylab = "Velocity",
  main = "Velocity Distribution by Cluster"
)

# Numerical descriptive measures side-by-side

# Make list of all measures
l <- list(
  sum_A = summary(cluster_a$VELOCITY),
  sum_b = summary(cluster_b$VELOCITY),
  IQR_a = IQR(cluster_a$VELOCITY),
  IQR_b = IQR(cluster_b$VELOCITY),
  sd_a = sd(cluster_a$VELOCITY),
  sd_b = sd(cluster_b$VELOCITY)
)

# Print list to compare

4.

In order to find out to which the galaxy with a velocity 20,000 km/s likely belongs, I will use z-scores to see if it is an outlier of either cluster, and determine which cluster 95% CI captures this velocity value. The cluster 95% that captures this observation and is not an outlier of is likely to be the cluster it belongs to.

# Get z-scores
x <- 20000

if_cluster_a <- abs((x - mean(cluster_a$VELOCITY)) / sd(cluster_a$VELOCITY))
if_cluster_b <- abs((x - mean(cluster_b$VELOCITY)) / sd(cluster_b$VELOCITY))

# Determine if an outlier for either cluster (Z > 3)

if_cluster_a > 3
## [1] FALSE
if_cluster_b > 3
## [1] TRUE
# Determine bounds of mean +/- 2sd to see if x falls in interval

# 2sd intervals
CI_L_a <- mean(cluster_a$VELOCITY) - 2 * sd(cluster_a$VELOCITY)
CI_U_a <- mean(cluster_a$VELOCITY) + 2 * sd(cluster_a$VELOCITY)

CI_L_b <- mean(cluster_b$VELOCITY) - 2 * sd(cluster_b$VELOCITY)
CI_U_b <- mean(cluster_b$VELOCITY) + 2 * sd(cluster_b$VELOCITY)

# Does x fall within the intervals?
x > CI_L_a & x < CI_U_a # Cluster A
## [1] TRUE
x > CI_L_b & x < CI_U_b # Cluster B
## [1] FALSE

It appears that the galaxy that has a velocity 20,000 km/s likely belongs to Cluster A. This is supported by the fact this observation is not an outlier of Cluster A and is of Cluster B, and the 95% CI of Cluster A captures this observation while the 95% CI of Cluster B does not. In conclusion, this evidence supports the claim that this galaxy likely belongs to Cluster A.

5.

# Get the mean of the unclustered data
mean_un <- mean(galaxy$VELOCITY)

# Calculate the 1sd intervals
CI_L <- mean_un - 1 * sd(galaxy$VELOCITY)
CI_U <- mean_un + 1 * sd(galaxy$VELOCITY)

# Get number of how many measured velocities were within this interval
length(galaxy$VELOCITY[galaxy$VELOCITY > CI_L &
                         galaxy$VELOCITY < CI_U])
## [1] 29

There are 29 measured velocities within 1 standard deviation of the mean of the un-clustered data.
